a: After Saul died
t: After the death of a leader
p: The book opens the way Joshua and Judges do: with a leader's death and the question of who comes next.
b: The Hebrew begins "after the death of Saul," the same way Joshua begins "After the death of Moses" (Joshua 1:1) and Judges begins "After Joshua died" (Judges 1:1). Each time a new chapter of Israel's story starts with an empty place at the top. In Hebrew, 1 and 2 Samuel were one book, so this verse picks up directly from Saul's death on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31). While Saul was dying, David was in the south, rescuing his families from the Amalekites who had burned Ziklag (1 Samuel 30). The narrator makes sure we know where David was: far from the battle, with clean hands.

a: His clothes were torn and he had earth on his head
p: Torn clothes and dirt on the head were the signs of a messenger bringing news of disaster.
b: Mourners tore their clothes and threw dust on their heads (Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12). The scene repeats an earlier one almost word for word: after the battle at Aphek a Benjaminite ran to Shiloh "with his clothes torn and earth on his head" to tell Eli that the ark was taken and his sons were dead (1 Samuel 4:12). There the news killed Eli. Here the messenger himself will die. Whether the young man's grief is real or put on for David is part of the puzzle of the chapter.

a: I just happened to be up on Mount Gilboa
p: 1 Samuel 31 says Saul fell on his own sword. The Amalekite says he killed Saul. Was he lying?
b: In 1 Samuel 31:4 Saul's armor-bearer refuses to kill him, so Saul falls on his sword and dies, and his armor-bearer sees that he is dead. Here a stranger says he found Saul still alive, leaning on his spear, and killed him at his request. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, think the Amalekite lied: he found the body, took the crown and armlet, and made up a story to win a reward from Saul's rival (4:10 says he thought he brought good news). Others harmonize: Saul's own thrust did not kill him, and the Amalekite finished it. Josephus tells it this way (Antiquities 6.14.7). Some critical scholars see two separate traditions. The text does not settle it, and the narrator lets David judge the man by his own words (1:16).

a: I am an Amalekite
p: Saul lost the kingdom over Amalek. Now an Amalekite brings his crown to David.
b: Saul was rejected as king for sparing Amalek (1 Samuel 15:9–28), and in that chapter Samuel tore Saul's robe and said the LORD had torn the kingdom from him. David has just come from defeating Amalekite raiders (1 Samuel 30:17–18). So it is an Amalekite who claims to have ended Saul's life and carries the royal crown to David. The irony would not be lost on an Israelite listener. The Hebrew written text (Ketiv) has "and he said" where the reading tradition (Qere) has "and I said"; the sense is the same. Throughout these chapters the Plain follows the Qere where the two differ, as at 1:16 and 3:15, and gives a note or variant only where the meaning changes.

a: A spinning dizziness has taken hold of me
t: A rare word for Saul's last state
p: The word shavats appears only here. It may mean dizziness, cramp or agony.
b: The Hebrew noun shavats occurs nowhere else in the Bible. Jewish commentators linked it to a word for checkered or woven work and took it as cramp or convulsion; others connect it with dizziness or a swoon, and the Greek translators guessed at a "dreadful darkness." The point is clear enough: Saul says he is badly hurt but still fully alive and cannot finish himself. The phrase "all my life is still in me" is awkward Hebrew, and translations vary.

a: the crown from his head and the band from his arm
p: Royal symbols that could pass the kingship on. The Amalekite hands them to Saul's rival.
b: The nezer was a royal headband or diadem, a sign that a king was set apart (2 Kings 11:12; Psalm 89:39). The ets'adah was an armlet; Assyrian reliefs show kings wearing heavy bands on the upper arm. By bringing them to David, the man treats David as Saul's heir and expects to be rewarded. David will later wear the crown of the Ammonite king (12:30). Whatever the truth of the man's story, Saul's crown now lies in David's hands, though David did nothing to take it.

a: I am the son of a resident foreigner, an Amalekite
p: A ger was a foreigner settled in Israel. He would have known Israel's ways, including respect for the king.
b: The word ger means a foreigner who lives among Israel under its protection (Exodus 22:21; Leviticus 19:34). This man was no stranger from the desert: his family lived in Israel, so he knew what Israelites believed about the LORD's anointed king. That is why David can hold him to account (1:14). Israel's law applied to the resident foreigner in matters of life and death (Leviticus 24:16–22).

a: the LORD's anointed
p: Hebrew meshiach YHWH. Saul's title is the root of the later word "Messiah."
b: Mashiach means "anointed one," someone marked out for a task by having oil poured on his head (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13). In Samuel the title belongs to the king God has chosen. David refused to kill Saul twice because he was "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9), and he now judges this man by the same rule. Through the Greek christos the word later became "Messiah" and "Christ," the hoped-for anointed king of David's line. In 2 Samuel it still means the reigning king, not yet a future figure (compare 19:21; 22:51; 23:1).
r: 1 Samuel 24:6; 1 Samuel 26:9; 2 Samuel 19:21; 2 Samuel 22:51; 2 Samuel 23:1; Psalm 2:2

a: Your blood is on your head
p: David executes the man on his own confession. Some readers see justice, others political cover.
b: "Your blood is on your head" means "you are responsible for your own death" (Joshua 2:19; 1 Kings 2:37). David condemns the man on his own claim, without testing it, since a confession of killing the king needed no further witness in his eyes. Traditional readers see David's loyalty: he would not reward anyone for touching the LORD's anointed. Critical historians such as McCarter and Halpern read the story as royal apology: by killing the one man who claimed Saul's death, David shows Israel that he had no part in it. Both readings notice that it served David well.

a: David raised this lament
t: A qinah, a song for the dead
p: David's lament follows the form of a qinah, the mourning song sung over the dead.
b: The verb and noun come from the same root: David "laments with this lament" (vayqonen ... haqqinah). A qinah was a dirge, often sung by women and by professional mourners (Jeremiah 9:17–20), with the cry "How!" (eikh). David's song for Saul and Jonathan is the most famous in the Bible. It never mentions God, never mentions Saul's sins, and never mentions David's long years as Saul's hunted enemy.

a: the song called "The Bow."
t: "The Bow": a title or a lesson?
p: The Hebrew says David said "to teach the sons of Judah bow." What "bow" means here is debated.
b: Literally: "and he said to teach the sons of Judah bow." Three readings are common. (1) "The Bow" is the name of the song, from Jonathan's bow in 1:22; most modern translations take it so. (2) David ordered Judah to be trained in archery after the defeat by Philistine archers (1 Samuel 31:3); the King James Version supplies "the use of the bow." (3) The word is a catchword or musical note that crept into the text. The main Greek text supports this view, since it has no word for "bow" (see the variant). Since 1:22 names the bow, the first view is still the most natural for the Hebrew.

a: the Book of Jashar
p: A lost collection of Israel's songs, quoted also in Joshua 10:13.
b: Sefer hayyashar means "the Book of the Upright" (or "of the Brave"). It was a collection of old poems, now lost. It is quoted for Joshua's command to the sun (Joshua 10:12–13), and the Greek text of 1 Kings 8:53 cites a "book of the song" (Hebrew shir, a near-match for yashar) for Solomon's words at the temple. Books named "Jasher" printed since the Middle Ages, including a Hebrew midrash of 1625 and an English forgery of 1751, are not the ancient book.

a: Your splendor, Israel
p: Hebrew tsevi means both "beauty, splendor" and "gazelle."
b: The song opens with hatstsevi, "the splendor" or "the gazelle." Both make sense. "Splendor" fits a nation's pride lying dead on the hills; this is how the Latin (Incliti Israhel) and the King James Version ("the beauty of Israel") take it. The Greek read the letters differently, as a command, "Set up a pillar, Israel" (see the variant). "Gazelle" suggests a swift young warrior, perhaps Jonathan, who lies slain "on your heights" in 1:25; the same word describes Asahel's speed in 2:18. The Plain keeps "splendor," and readers may hear the gazelle beneath it.

a: How the warriors have fallen!
p: The cry comes three times: at the start, near the end, and as the last line.
b: "How the warriors have fallen" (eikh naflu gibborim) frames the song (1:19, 1:25, 1:27) and marks off its three parts: the long first part for Saul and Jonathan together, the short second part for Jonathan alone, and the closing line. The English phrase "How are the mighty fallen" (KJV) has become proverbial. Gibborim are warriors, heroes, men of strength. Each time the line returns, the song narrows: Israel's splendor, then Jonathan, then the weapons of war themselves. When Judas Maccabeus fell in battle in 160 BC, all Israel mourned him with the same cry: "How the warrior has fallen, / the one who saved Israel!" (1 Maccabees 9:21).

a: Do not tell it in Gath
p: Philistine cities would celebrate Saul's death. Micah later echoes the line.
b: Gath and Ashkelon stand for all of Philistia. In Israel, women sang to greet returning victors (1 Samuel 18:6–7; Exodus 15:20); David does not want Philistine women singing over Israel's dead. Nearly three centuries later the prophet Micah opens his lament over Judah's towns with the same words, "In Gath do not tell it" (Micah 1:10), so the line had become a byword. "The uncircumcised" is Israel's scornful name for the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:26; 1 Samuel 31:4).

a: may your fields bear nothing to offer
p: The Hebrew says "fields of offerings," an odd phrase. Some read a different text.
b: The Hebrew sede terumot means "fields of contributions," that is, fields that yield grain to offer as gifts. As a curse it asks that Gilboa produce nothing worth offering. The phrase is strange, and in 1938 H. L. Ginsberg proposed reading sera' tehomot, "the welling up of the deeps," because a Canaanite curse from Ugarit pairs "no dew, no rain" with "no surging of the deeps" (see the next note). No manuscript has that reading, so the Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: may no dew and no rain come down on you
t: A curse on the land where the hero fell
p: A Canaanite poem from Ugarit has a father curse the land where his son was killed, in very similar words.
b: In the Ugaritic story of Aqhat (about 1300 BC), when the young hero Aqhat is murdered, his father Danel curses the places linked to his death and prays that for seven years Baal will send "no dew, no rain, no surging of the two deeps." David's lament likewise curses the mountains where Saul and Jonathan fell. The parallel is real and shows that David's song uses the shared poetic language of Canaan. It does not show borrowing of belief: David curses the place out of grief, and calls on no god of rain.

a: with no oil to anoint it
p: Leather shields were rubbed with oil. The word for "anointed" also recalls Saul's title.
b: Shields of hide were oiled to keep them supple and to make blows slide off (Isaiah 21:5). Saul's shield now lies in the dirt, unoiled. The Hebrew beli mashiach, "not anointed," can also be read of Saul himself, as the King James Version does: "as though he had not been anointed with oil." The word mashiach was Saul's royal title (1:14), so the poem lets both meanings sound: the king anointed by God dies like any man.

a: in their lives and in their deaths were never torn apart
p: David praises father and son as one, though Saul once tried to kill Jonathan.
b: Saul hurled a spear at Jonathan for taking David's side (1 Samuel 20:30–33), yet Jonathan fought and died beside his father on Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:2). David honors that loyalty. The Hebrew accents put a break after "in their lives": "beloved and pleasant in their lives, and in their death not parted." Either way, the song chooses to remember Saul at his best. Many readers find this generosity the most moving thing about David in the whole book.

a: He dressed you in scarlet and luxury
p: Saul's wars brought wealth home. Israel's women had worn the plunder.
b: Red-dyed cloth was costly, and gold ornaments came home as spoil from victories (Judges 5:30; Judges 8:24–26). In the song the women who should have been singing victory songs over the Philistines (1:20) are told to weep over the king who once made them rich. David asks Israel to remember what Saul gave them, not what he took.

a: more than the love of women
p: Was this deep friendship, a political bond, or a romance? Readers have argued all three.
b: Jonathan "loved David as himself" (1 Samuel 18:1–3), and the two made a covenant. The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian, sees the Bible's great friendship: the Mishnah holds it up as love that does not depend on any selfish cause (Avot 5:16). A political reading notes that "love" in treaties meant loyalty between allies, so Jonathan, the crown prince, gave up his claim to David (J. A. Thompson). Some modern readers (Tom Horner, and in a more cautious way Susan Ackerman) see erotic love. Others, such as Saul Olyan and Robert Gagnon, answer that the words fit intense friendship in that culture, and that nothing in the text describes a sexual bond. The Hebrew "wonderful" (nifle'ah) and the comparison with women's love leave the question to the reader. See the notes on 1 Samuel 18:1–3 and 20:41.

a: The weapons of war are lost
p: The "weapons of war" are probably Saul and Jonathan themselves.
b: The song has spoken of Jonathan's bow and Saul's sword and shield (1:21–22). In the last line the "weapons of war" most likely stand for the two warriors, Israel's defense now broken, as Isaiah calls the Persians God's "weapons" (Isaiah 13:5). Some read the line literally of the arms left on Gilboa and hung in a Philistine temple (1 Samuel 31:10). The song ends on loss, with no word of hope.

a: David asked the LORD for guidance
p: David consults God, probably through the priest Abiathar and the ephod with the Urim.
b: The verb sha'al "ask" is the usual word for consulting God by lot through a priest. Abiathar had brought the ephod to David (1 Samuel 23:6–9), and David asked by it before chasing the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30:7–8). The answers come one word at a time, "Go up," "Hebron," as yes-or-no and simple-choice questions would. David's first act as a free man is to ask, where Saul in his last days got no answer at all (1 Samuel 28:6).

a: "Hebron," he said
p: Judah's chief town, tied to Abraham and Caleb, and already friendly to David.
b: Hebron sat high in the hills of Judah, about 19 miles south of Jerusalem. Abraham was buried there with Sarah, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 23:19; Genesis 49:29–31), and Caleb won it in the conquest (Joshua 14:13–14). David had married into the Calebite clan through Abigail (1 Samuel 25:3, 25:42), and he had sent gifts from the Amalekite spoil to Hebron's elders (1 Samuel 30:26–31). It was a natural capital for a king of Judah. David will rule there seven and a half years (2:11).

a: there they anointed David to be king over Judah's house
p: Samuel anointed David in private. Now the men of Judah anoint him in public. All Israel will follow (5:3).
b: David is anointed three times. Samuel anointed him secretly in Bethlehem as a boy (1 Samuel 16:13). Here his own tribe makes him king. Later the elders of all Israel anoint him at Hebron (5:3). The steps show the book's view of how God's choice becomes reality: through the people's consent, slowly, without David seizing it. "House of Judah" names the tribe as one family; the phrase first appears here and becomes a political name.

a: You have done this act of loyal love for your lord
p: Hebrew hesed: loyalty that goes beyond duty. The men of Jabesh showed it to Saul.
b: Hesed is rendered "loyal love" throughout this translation. It is faithfulness inside a relationship, kept even when it costs. The men of Jabesh-gilead risked their lives to take Saul's body from the wall of Beth-shan, because Saul had once rescued their town (1 Samuel 11:1–11; 1 Samuel 31:11–13). David blesses their hesed and asks God to show them the same. Hesed is a key word in chapters 2, 3, 9 and 10: Abner claims it (3:8), David shows it to Mephibosheth (9:1, 9:3, 9:7) and offers it to Hanun (10:2).

a: Your lord Saul is dead, and as for me
p: David's message honors Jabesh and also asks it to accept him as king.
b: The letter thanks Jabesh, then adds that Judah has anointed David. Jabesh lay in Gilead, the region Abner soon claims for Ish-bosheth (2:9). Many readers see sincere gratitude joined to sound politics. Critical scholars stress the politics: David is recruiting Saul's most loyal town. The text does not say how Jabesh answered. Years later David honors Saul's and Jonathan's bones by taking them from Jabesh to their family tomb (21:12–14).

a: Ish-bosheth
p: His real name was probably Eshbaal or Ishbaal. Later scribes replaced "baal" with "shame."
b: Chronicles calls Saul's son Eshbaal, "man of Baal" (1 Chronicles 8:33; 1 Chronicles 9:39), and Jonathan's son Merib-baal (1 Chronicles 8:34), whom Samuel calls Mephibosheth (4:4). In Samuel the element baal has been replaced by bosheth, "shame," as in Jerubbaal and Jerubbesheth (Judges 6:32; 11:21) and as the prophets called Baal "the shameful thing" (Jeremiah 3:24; Hosea 9:10). Baal means "lord" and could once be used of the LORD himself (Hosea 2:16), so Saul probably meant no disloyalty. A jar inscription from Khirbet Qeiyafa, from about 1000 BC, bears the name "Eshbaal son of Beda," showing the name was in use at the time. The Plain keeps the traditional spelling.
r: 1 Chronicles 8:33–34; 1 Chronicles 9:39–40; Judges 6:32; 2 Samuel 11:21; Jeremiah 3:24; Hosea 2:16; Hosea 9:10

a: Mahanaim
p: Abner set up Saul's son east of the Jordan, out of reach of the Philistines.
b: Mahanaim, "two camps," was in Gilead, near the Jabbok River, where Jacob once met God's angels (Genesis 32:2). After Gilboa the Philistines held the Jezreel Valley and much of the west (1 Samuel 31:7), so Saul's house ruled from the far side of the Jordan. David himself will take refuge at Mahanaim when Absalom rebels (17:24–27), and Absalom's death is reported to him there.

a: forty years old
p: Ish-bosheth reigned two years while David reigned seven and a half in Hebron. The numbers are hard to fit.
b: If Ish-bosheth was forty, he was older than David, which some find hard to square with his absence from Gilboa. Saul's list of sons in 1 Samuel 14:49 does not name him either, though many scholars think its "Ishvi" is the same man, a form of Ishyo or Ishbaal. And his two years do not match David's seven and a half at Hebron (2:11; 5:5). Suggested solutions: some years passed before Abner could make him king, after the Philistines withdrew; or David stayed at Hebron for several years after Ish-bosheth's death before taking Jerusalem; or the numbers, like those for Saul in 1 Samuel 13:1, were damaged in copying. Each is possible; none is proven.

a: the servants of Saul's son Ish-bosheth
p: The same Hebrew word means servant, official, soldier or slave. Context decides.
b: Eved covers everyone who serves another: a slave (Exodus 21:2), a king's officer or soldier (here and 2:13, 2:17), a vassal nation (8:2, 8:6, 8:14), and anyone speaking humbly to a superior, as David does to God ("your servant," ten times in 7:18–29) and Mephibosheth to David (9:8). In this book Abner's and Joab's "servants" are their fighting men. The Plain uses "servant" where the sense is service or humble address, and "slave" only where a person is owned.

a: the pool of Gibeon
p: Excavators at el-Jib found a huge rock-cut pool with a spiral stairway. Many identify it with this pool.
b: Gibeon, about 6 miles north of Jerusalem, is the modern village of el-Jib; jar handles inscribed with the name Gibeon were found there. James Pritchard's excavations (1956–1962) uncovered a round shaft about 37 feet across and 35 feet deep, cut into the rock, with a stairway winding down and continuing to a water chamber below. Pritchard identified it with the pool of this verse and of Jeremiah 41:12. Some scholars think the shaft is later than David; others accept the link. Either way, Gibeon had a famous pool.

a: put on a contest for us
p: Hebrew sachaq "play, sport." A duel of picked fighters was meant to settle the matter with fewer deaths.
b: The verb sachaq means to play, to make sport, even to dance (6:5, 6:21). Abner proposes a duel of champions, twelve from each side, as Goliath had once proposed a single combat (1 Samuel 17:8–9). Yigael Yadin compared a relief from Tell Halaf in Syria that shows pairs of fighters, each gripping the other's head and stabbing him in the side, exactly as in 2:16. The "game" ends with everyone dead and settles nothing, and a full battle follows.

a: Helkath-hazzurim
p: The name probably means "field of blades" or "field of flints." The Greek has a different name.
b: Chelqat means "portion, field." Hatstsurim may mean "the flints" (blades were once made of flint, Joshua 5:2) or "the sides," from the stab wounds in the side. The Greek translators read a slightly different word and called it "the portion of the plotters," as if the duel had been a trap. Place names in Samuel often keep the memory of an event, like Baal-perazim (5:20) and Perez-uzzah (6:8).

a: Asahel could run like one of the gazelles
p: The same word as "splendor" in David's lament. Asahel's speed will be his death.
b: Tsevi, gazelle, is the word that opened David's lament (1:19). Speed was a warrior's praise (1:23; 22:34; 1 Chronicles 12:8). Asahel, Joab's youngest brother, wants the glory of killing the enemy commander. His speed brings him to Abner, and his refusal to turn aside kills him. His death starts the blood feud that leads to Abner's murder (3:27, 3:30).

a: take his armor for yourself
p: Abner tells Asahel to take the gear of some ordinary soldier and leave the commander alone.
b: The word means what is stripped from a fallen enemy: armor, weapons, clothes (Judges 14:19). Abner, the older and more skilled fighter, offers Asahel a trophy that would still bring honor without the risk. Twice he warns him (2:21–22). Abner knows that killing Joab's brother will start a blood feud he cannot win (2:22), and he is right.

a: the back end of his spear
t: The butt of the spear and the "fifth rib"
p: Abner struck with the spear's back end. The King James Version's "fifth rib" is an old misreading.
b: Spears often had a pointed metal butt so they could be stuck upright in the ground (1 Samuel 26:7). Abner did not turn and aim; he thrust backward with the butt, and Asahel's own speed drove it through him. Some think Abner hoped only to stop him. The word for where he struck, chomesh, means the belly; older interpreters linked it to chamesh, "five," so the King James Version says "under the fifth rib." The same word comes in 3:27, 4:6 (in the Hebrew) and 20:10. The Talmud weighs this death when Solomon judges Joab: Joab argues that Asahel was a pursuer whom Abner had the right to kill, and the answer is that Abner could have stopped him by wounding a limb, so Abner was still to blame (Bavli Sanhedrin 49a). The case shows how seriously the rabbis took the question of whether Joab's revenge was lawful.

a: stopped and stood still
p: Men stop at the body. The same thing happens when Amasa dies in 20:12.
b: Soldiers coming up from behind stopped where Asahel lay, so the pursuit lost its force. The scene is repeated when Joab kills Amasa and the troops stop at his body in the road (20:12). The two deaths frame Joab's career: his brother's death here, and the men Joab himself kills later (3:27; 20:10).

a: Will the sword keep eating forever?
p: Abner pleads for an end to civil war among brothers.
b: The sword that "eats" flesh is an old image (Deuteronomy 32:42; Jeremiah 46:10). Abner, who started the contest (2:14), now calls for peace: the dead are "brothers." Israel had once nearly destroyed Benjamin in a civil war (Judges 20–21), and the bitterness of that war was remembered. Joab agrees, but he will not forget Asahel.

a: if you had not said a word
p: Joab's answer can mean the fighting would have stopped in the morning, or gone on until morning.
b: Joab's oath is compressed. (1) If Abner had not proposed the "contest" (2:14), the troops would have gone home that morning without fighting. This reading, followed here, puts the blame on Abner. (2) If Abner had not called out now, the pursuit would have gone on until morning; on this view Joab grants that Abner's plea has saved lives. The Hebrew "from the morning" can bear either sense.

a: the whole Bithron
t: Bithron: a ravine or a morning?
p: Bithron may be a valley name, "the ravine," or a word for the forenoon.
b: Bitron comes from a root meaning "to cut in two." Many take it as a gorge east of the Jordan leading to Mahanaim, hence a proper name. Others take it as "the forenoon," a half of the day, matching the march "all night" before it: they walked all night and all the next morning. Either fits the speed of the retreat.

a: nineteen men were missing, and Asahel
p: Twenty on David's side, 360 on Abner's: the narrator lets the numbers show who was winning.
b: David's losses are small, but one of them is Joab's brother, named apart from the rest. Abner's losses are eighteen times greater, all from Benjamin, Saul's own tribe (2:31). The figures prepare for 3:1: David's house growing stronger, Saul's growing weaker.

a: the tomb of his father at Bethlehem
p: Zeruiah's family came from Bethlehem, David's town.
b: Zeruiah was David's sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), so Asahel was David's nephew. His father is never named; the sons are always called by their mother's name, perhaps because she was the link to David. Family tombs were cut in the rock outside a town, and bones were gathered there over generations (21:14; Genesis 49:29–31). Joab's night march on to Hebron, another 14 miles or so, matches Abner's night march to Mahanaim (2:29).

a: the war between Saul's house and David's house
p: "House" means family and dynasty. The word runs through chapters 1–7 until God promises David a house.
b: Hebrew bayit means a building, a household and a royal line. The war is between two "houses," Saul's line and David's. The word keeps returning: the "house of Judah" (2:4), Abner strengthening himself "in Saul's house" (3:6), David's "house" of cedar (5:11; 7:2), God's "house" (7:5), and finally God's promise to make David a "house" that lasts forever (7:11, 7:16). The verse's two lines, one growing and one shrinking, sum up chapters 2–5.
orig: בֵּית שָׁאוּל ... בֵּית דָּוִד (beit Sha'ul ... beit David)

a: sons were born to him
t: David's sons and wives at Hebron
p: Six sons from six wives. Several marriages were political alliances.
b: Each son has a different mother. Ahinoam and Abigail had been with David in the wilderness (1 Samuel 25:42–43). Maacah was a king's daughter from Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee; the marriage gave David an ally on Ish-bosheth's northern flank. Jon Levenson and Baruch Halpern argued that David's marriages also tied him to powerful clans in Judah, and that Ahinoam may be the same person as Saul's wife Ahinoam (1 Samuel 14:50; compare 2 Samuel 12:8). Most commentators find that last idea possible but unproven. Deuteronomy warned the king, "He must not take many wives for himself" (Deuteronomy 17:17). Three of these sons, Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah, will die in the struggles of chapters 13–18 and 1 Kings 1–2.

a: Absalom, the son of Maacah, the daughter of King Talmai of Geshur
p: Absalom will flee to his grandfather in Geshur after killing Amnon.
b: This short line prepares for a long story. When Absalom kills his half-brother Amnon, he runs to his mother's father, Talmai king of Geshur, and stays three years (13:37–38). Absalom's sister Tamar is also Maacah's daughter (13:1). Geshur lay in the Golan, east of the Sea of Galilee, and Israel never drove it out (Joshua 13:13).

a: Adonijah, Haggith's son
p: The fourth son will claim the throne in David's old age.
b: After Amnon and Absalom are dead, Adonijah, the oldest surviving son, makes himself king while David lies dying, and is outmaneuvered by Nathan and Bathsheba on Solomon's behalf (1 Kings 1:5–53). He later asks for David's last companion, Abishag, as wife, and Solomon has him killed (1 Kings 2:13–25). Chileab, the second son, is never heard of again; many assume he died young.

a: Why have you gone to bed with my father's concubine?
t: A king's concubine and a claim to the throne
p: To take a dead king's concubine was a claim to his place. Ish-bosheth sees a threat.
b: A concubine was a wife of lower rank (Genesis 22:24; Judges 19:1). In the ancient Near East a new king took over his predecessor's harem. So when Reuben slept with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22; 49:4), when Absalom went in to David's concubines on the palace roof (16:21–22), and when Adonijah asked for Abishag (1 Kings 2:22), each act was a claim to the father's place. Whether Abner really did it the Masoretic Text does not say, and Abner does not deny it. The Lucianic Greek, and 4QSam-a as reported, add "and Abner took her" (see the variant). Rizpah appears again in one of the most moving scenes in the book (21:8–14).

a: So I am a dog's head, am I, one that belongs to Judah?
p: A strong insult: "Am I a worthless traitor working for Judah?"
b: Dogs in Israel were scavengers, not pets, and "dog" was a word of contempt (1 Samuel 17:43; 1 Samuel 24:14; 9:8; 16:9). "A dog's head" occurs only here and seems to mean the lowest of the low. "Belonging to Judah" makes it treason: "Do you take me for a dog in Judah's pay?" Abner's outrage is ironic, since in the next breath he offers Israel to David. The Greek has only "Am I a dog's head?" and lacks "one that belongs to Judah," which may be an explanatory addition in the Hebrew.

a: God do this to Abner, and more besides
p: "May God punish me severely if I don't." The speaker invokes a curse on himself.
b: The formula, "So may God do to X and so may he add," was probably spoken with a gesture, as if to say "May God do this to me, and worse." It is used by Eli (1 Samuel 3:17), Saul (1 Samuel 14:44), Jonathan (1 Samuel 20:13) and David (1 Samuel 25:22; 3:35). Abner swears by it in the third person, using his own name.
orig: כֹּה־יַעֲשֶׂה אֱלֹהִים לְאַבְנֵר וְכֹה יֹסִיף לוֹ (koh ya'aseh Elohim le'Avner vekhoh yosif lo)

a: what the LORD swore to him
p: No such oath is recorded in so many words. Abner knows what everyone knew: the kingdom was promised to David.
b: Samuel told Saul that the LORD had torn the kingdom from him and given it to a neighbor better than he (1 Samuel 15:28), and anointed David (1 Samuel 16:13). Jonathan said that David would be king (1 Samuel 23:17), Saul himself admitted it (1 Samuel 24:20), and Abigail spoke of the LORD's promise to make David ruler (1 Samuel 25:30). Abner, Saul's own commander, now speaks of it as an oath. The book's point is that even Saul's men knew whom God had chosen.

a: all the way from Dan to Beersheba
p: The standard way of saying "the whole land," from the far north to the far south.
b: Dan lay at the foot of Mount Hermon near the springs of the Jordan; Beersheba lay at the edge of the Negev desert. The phrase means all Israel (Judges 20:1; 1 Samuel 3:20; 17:11; 24:2). Abner offers David everything Saul ruled.

a: to speak for him
p: A difficult phrase: Abner sent messengers "in his place," "on the spot," or "to Hebron, where David was."
b: The Hebrew tachtav (written text tachto) means "under him" or "in his place." It may mean "on his behalf," as rendered here, or "at once, on the spot." The main Greek text reads "to Thaelam, where he was, at once," taking the word as a place name; the Lucianic Greek has "to Hebron, where he was." The same word comes with a written-and-read difference in 2:23, where it means "on the spot."

a: Who does the land belong to?
p: A blunt bargaining line. Abner may mean "The land is yours" or "The land is mine to give."
b: Abner's question is short and unclear. Some take it as "Who else should the land belong to but you?" Others as "Who controls the land? I do," a reminder that Abner holds the real power in the north. Both fit the bargain that follows: a covenant with Abner, and Abner will bring Israel. The scene shows how David's kingdom was built through negotiation as well as by God's promise.

a: unless you bring Saul's daughter Michal
p: Love, a broken bargain, or a claim to Saul's throne? Readers have seen all three.
b: Saul had given Michal to David for a bride-price of Philistine foreskins (1 Samuel 18:20–27), and later "handed his daughter Michal, who was David's wife, to Palti son of Laish from Gallim" (1 Samuel 25:44). A political reading, common among critical scholars, sees David reclaiming a royal wife who made him Saul's son-in-law and strengthened his claim to Saul's throne. A legal reading notes that David had paid the bride-price and never divorced her. Readers who look for feeling note that the text says Michal once loved David (1 Samuel 18:20), but never says David loved her. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 forbids remarrying a divorced wife who has married another man; Jewish commentators answered that David had never divorced Michal, so the law did not apply.

a: a hundred Philistine foreskins
p: Saul asked for a hundred; David brought two hundred. David names the price Saul set.
b: Saul demanded a hundred Philistine foreskins as Michal's bride-price, hoping David would be killed (1 Samuel 18:25). The Masoretic Text says David "struck down two hundred of the Philistines" (1 Samuel 18:27); the Greek there says a hundred. Here David names the agreed price, the legal basis of his claim. He sends this demand to Ish-bosheth, not to Abner, so that the return of Michal is an official act of Saul's house.

a: He walked behind her crying, all the way to Bahurim
p: Michal says nothing. Her second husband weeps after her until Abner sends him home.
b: The only person in the scene who shows feeling is Paltiel (called Palti in 1 Samuel 25:44). Michal herself is silent, handed from man to man. The Talmud praises Paltiel, saying he never touched Michal because he knew she was still David's wife, and that he planted a sword between them (Bavli Sanhedrin 19b). Feminist readers such as Cheryl Exum see Michal as a woman used by both Saul and David for political ends, whose own voice is heard only in bitterness (6:20). Bahurim, near Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan, is the border of Benjamin; it will appear again with Shimei (16:5).

a: you have been trying to get David made king over you
p: Abner admits that Israel's elders had long wanted David.
b: "Yesterday and the day before" is the Hebrew idiom for "for some time now." David's victories had made him popular across Israel (1 Samuel 18:7, 18:16). Abner now uses that popularity as a lever with the elders, and he gives a religious reason as well (3:18). The tribal elders, not just the army, had to agree to a king (5:3).

a: Through David my servant I will rescue my people Israel
p: God once said Saul would rescue Israel from the Philistines. Now the same task is David's.
b: When God sent Saul to Samuel, he said, "He will rescue my people from the Philistines' grip" (1 Samuel 9:16). Abner now applies that promise to David. No oracle in these exact words is recorded, so Abner may be quoting freely from what he knew (see 3:9). "My servant David" will become a lasting title, used by God in 7:5 and 7:8 and by the prophets for a coming king (Ezekiel 34:23; Ezekiel 37:24).

a: and he left in peace
p: The phrase is repeated three times (3:21, 3:22, 3:23) just before Abner is murdered.
b: The narrator stresses that David sent Abner away "in peace," and repeats it twice more, once in his own voice and once in the report to Joab. The repetition clears David of what is about to happen, and it makes Joab's act a breach of the king's peace. Hebrew shalom means safety and well-being as well as the end of war.

a: when you go out and when you come in
p: A pair of opposites meaning "all your movements, everything you do."
b: Hebrew often says "all" by naming two ends of a range. "Your going out and your coming in" covers all of a person's affairs, including war (1 Samuel 18:13, 18:16; Psalm 121:8; Deuteronomy 28:6). Joab claims that Abner came as a spy. He may believe it; he may also fear that Abner, a famous commander, would replace him at the head of the army.

a: into the middle of the gate
t: Murder in the gate of Hebron
p: Hebron was a city of refuge, where blood-vengeance was supposed to be checked.
b: The city gate was the public place where elders judged and business was done (Ruth 4:1–11). Joab draws Abner aside there as if for a private word. The Greek has him take Abner aside "from the gate," that is, to one side of it, rather than into its middle. Hebron was one of the cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7), where a killer was safe from the avenger of blood until his case was heard (Numbers 35:9–28). Asahel died in battle, and Abner had warned him twice, so by Israel's law Abner was not a murderer. Jewish and Christian commentators have often pointed out that Joab took revenge in the one place where it was most clearly forbidden.

a: my kingdom and I are clean of the blood of Abner son of Ner for all time
p: The narrator insists that David had no part in Abner's death. Some historians suspect otherwise.
b: The text works hard to clear David: he sent Abner away in peace (3:21–23), "David knew nothing about it" (3:26), he cursed Joab (3:29), mourned publicly (3:31–35), and "all Israel understood" he was innocent (3:37). Traditional readers take this at face value: David lost his best chance of a peaceful union by Abner's death. Some critical historians, notably James VanderKam, McCarter and Halpern, ask why so much defense was needed, and suggest that the story answers rumors that David profited from the deaths of Saul, Abner and Ish-bosheth. Shimei will later call David "a man of blood" (16:7–8). The text gives evidence for both readings, but it plainly wants the reader to believe David.

a: who grip a spindle
p: Hebrew pelekh can mean a spindle, women's work, or a staff that a lame man leans on.
b: David's curse lists disgraces: a bodily discharge that made a man unclean (Leviticus 15:2), skin disease (Leviticus 13), "holding the pelekh," death by the sword and hunger. Pelekh means a spindle in Proverbs 31:19, so many read "a man fit only to spin," an insult to a warrior's manhood. Others read "a crutch," as the King James Version does ("that leaneth on a staff"), matching the sick and disabled in the list. In this translation tsara'at is always "skin disease," not leprosy, since the Hebrew word covers many conditions.

a: Wrap yourselves in sackcloth
p: Torn clothes, sackcloth and a public procession: David orders full mourning, even for Joab.
b: Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn against the skin in grief (Genesis 37:34; 1 Kings 21:27). The bier was an open frame on which the body was carried (Luke 7:14). David makes Joab himself tear his clothes and walk before the body of the man he killed. The king walking behind the bier is a public sign of honor and grief, and of his own innocence.

a: Did Abner have to die the way a fool dies?
p: Hebrew naval: a fool who brings ruin on himself. Abner died helplessly, not in battle.
b: A naval is a godless or senseless man; Nabal, Abigail's husband, bore the name and died by his own folly (1 Samuel 25:25, 25:38). David's short lament says Abner should not have died like a fool or a criminal. His hands were free and his feet unchained (3:34): he was killed by a trick, not taken prisoner or beaten in fair fight. "Crooked men," literally "sons of injustice," are the treacherous.

a: if I eat any bread, or anything else, before sundown
p: Mourners fasted until evening. David refuses the meal friends brought to comfort him.
b: Israel fasted for the dead until sunset (1:12) and sometimes for seven days (1 Samuel 31:13). Friends brought bread to mourners to end the fast (Jeremiah 16:7; Ezekiel 24:17). David refuses until evening. The people notice and approve (3:36). When his own child is dying, David will fast before the death and eat after it, shocking his servants (12:16–23).

a: these men, Zeruiah's sons, are too harsh for me
t: David and the sons of Zeruiah
p: David admits he cannot control Joab and Abishai. He leaves vengeance to the LORD, and later to Solomon.
b: "Soft" (rakh) means tender or weak. David's nephews are "hard" (qashim). The complaint returns: "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?" (16:10; 19:22). Some readers see a king rightly leaving vengeance to God. Others see weakness or calculation: David needed Joab, and Joab kept command for his whole reign. On his deathbed David tells Solomon to deal with Joab for the blood of Abner and Amasa (1 Kings 2:5–6), and Solomon does (1 Kings 2:28–34).

a: His hands went limp
p: A Hebrew idiom for losing heart.
b: "His hands dropped" means his courage failed (Isaiah 13:7; Jeremiah 6:24; Zephaniah 3:16). Ish-bosheth's strength had been Abner. The text does not even name him in this verse, only "Saul's son" (see the variant), as if he no longer counts.

a: sons of Rimmon of Beeroth
p: Beeroth was one of the four Gibeonite towns. Its people may have had a grudge against Saul's house.
b: Beeroth was one of the Gibeonite cities that made peace with Joshua (Joshua 9:17) and lay in Benjamin's land (Joshua 18:25). The note that its people fled to Gittaim (4:3) may reflect Saul's violence against the Gibeonites, which 21:1–2 mentions without details. If so, the two brothers may have had family reasons as well as ambition for killing Saul's son. The text does not say.

a: Mephibosheth
p: Jonathan's son is called Merib-baal in Chronicles. Samuel replaces "baal" with "shame."
b: Chronicles names him Merib-baal, perhaps "Baal is advocate" or "hero of Baal" (1 Chronicles 8:34; 1 Chronicles 9:40). As with Ish-bosheth (2:8), Samuel's text replaces baal with bosheth, "shame." The verse interrupts the story to tell us that Jonathan's heir is a crippled child. With Ish-bosheth dead, no son of Saul with a real claim and a following is left. Saul did still have descendants: two sons by his concubine Rizpah, Armoni and another Mephibosheth, and five grandsons through a daughter (21:8). But sons of a concubine had a weaker claim, and none of them had Abner's army behind him. The story of how David treats him follows in chapter 9.

a: while he lay resting at noon
p: In the heat of the day everyone slept, even the guards.
b: In the Near East work stopped in the hottest hours and people rested (Genesis 18:1). The assassins come when the house is quiet. A king who naps unguarded at noon contrasts with David, whose servants rouse him in the night (and who will later rise from his couch in the evening, 11:2). The narrator gives no sign of how long Ish-bosheth had reigned (2:10).

a: The LORD has let my lord the king take revenge today
p: The killers claim God was on their side. David answers that God is not served by murder.
b: The brothers bring the head as David once brought Goliath's head to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 17:54). They use pious language: Ish-bosheth was David's enemy, and the LORD has avenged him. David has heard this before (1:10). He answers with an oath by the LORD who has rescued him, and he does not accept a gift won by murder. The story ends the line of men who expected to profit from killing Saul's house.

a: who has set my life free from every kind of trouble
p: David swears by the God who rescued him, so he needs no assassins to rescue him.
b: The verb padah means to ransom or set free, as God ransomed Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). David will use the same oath on his deathbed (1 Kings 1:29). The point is pointed: God has kept David safe through all his troubles without help from murderers, and he does not need them now.

a: a man who did nothing wrong
p: Hebrew tsaddiq. Here it means innocent in the legal sense, not morally perfect.
b: Tsaddiq is often translated "righteous." In a legal setting it means the one in the right, the innocent party (Exodus 23:7; Deuteronomy 25:1). Ish-bosheth had done nothing to deserve death: he was killed in his bed in his own house. "Demand his blood" means to hold the killers responsible for it, as God demands a life for a life (Genesis 9:5).

a: They cut off their hands and their feet and hung them up
p: The hands that killed and the feet that ran are cut off and shown in public.
b: The punishment fits the crime: the hands that struck Ish-bosheth and the feet that carried his head all night (4:7). Exposing a body was a public warning (Joshua 10:26; 1 Samuel 31:10). Deuteronomy required that a hanged body be taken down before night, "his body must not stay on the tree overnight" (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the text does not say how long these hung. Ish-bosheth's head is buried with honor in Abner's tomb, so the two who led Saul's house lie together at Hebron.

a: we are your own bone and flesh
p: A formula of kinship and loyalty, first heard when Adam greets Eve.
b: The man in Eden says of the woman, "This one at last is bone from my bones / and flesh from my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). Laban says it to Jacob (Genesis 29:14), and Abimelech uses it to win Shechem: "Remember, I am your own bone and flesh" (Judges 9:2). Walter Brueggemann argued that the phrase is a pledge of loyalty in good times and bad, almost a covenant formula. The tribes are saying more than "we are related": they are binding themselves to David. The covenant follows in 5:3.

a: You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel
p: Kings in the ancient world were called shepherds. David really had been one.
b: Mesopotamian kings called themselves shepherds of their people; Hammurabi does so in the prologue to his laws. In Israel the image has a double edge, because David was taken from the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11; 1 Samuel 17:34–35; 7:8; Psalm 78:70–72). Ezekiel condemns Israel's shepherds who fed themselves and promises "my servant David" as the one shepherd (Ezekiel 34:2–24). Micah's ruler from Bethlehem will shepherd his flock, a passage Matthew applies to Jesus (Micah 5:2–4; Matthew 2:6), and Jesus calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11).
r: 1 Samuel 16:11; 1 Samuel 17:34–35; 7:8; Psalm 78:70–72; Ezekiel 34:2–24; Micah 5:2–4; Matthew 2:6; John 10:11

a: You will be ruler over Israel
p: Nagid is the title for the leader God designates. Melekh, "king," is the title the people give.
b: Nagid is rendered "ruler" throughout this translation. God told Samuel to anoint Saul as nagid (1 Samuel 9:16; 1 Samuel 10:1), and David was named nagid in Saul's place (1 Samuel 13:14; 1 Samuel 25:30). In 5:3 the elders then make David melekh, "king." The two words show the two sides of kingship in Samuel: chosen by God, accepted by the people. David himself uses nagid of his calling (6:21), and God uses it in the great promise (7:8).

a: King David made a covenant with them
t: A covenant between king and people
p: The king bound himself to the tribes before they anointed him.
b: This covenant was an agreement that set the terms of David's rule, sworn "in the LORD's presence." Samuel had written "the rules of the kingship" in a scroll at Saul's accession (1 Samuel 10:25). Later, the northern tribes asked Rehoboam to lighten their load before they would accept him, and when he refused they left (1 Kings 12:1–16). Jehoiada made a covenant between king and people when Joash was crowned (2 Kings 11:17). Israel's king was not supposed to be an absolute ruler.

a: his reign lasted forty years
p: David's reign is usually dated about 1010–970 BC. Forty is also a round number for a full generation.
b: Saul (Acts 13:21), David and Solomon (1 Kings 11:42) are each given forty years. Forty often stands for a full generation (Judges 3:11; Judges 5:31), so some think the figure is rounded. David's thirty-three years in Jerusalem plus seven and a half in Hebron make forty and a half (5:5). Most chronologies place David's reign in the early 10th century BC. 1 Chronicles 29:27 gives the same numbers.

a: the Jebusites who lived in that land
p: Jerusalem was an old Canaanite city that Israel had never taken.
b: Jerusalem is named in Egyptian texts of the 1800s BC and in the Amarna letters of the 1300s BC, when its king Abdi-Heba wrote to Pharaoh. In Israel's story it was held by the Jebusites: "the Benjaminites did not drive them out" (Judges 1:21), and Judah could not drive them out either (Joshua 15:63). It lay on the border between Judah and Benjamin, belonging to neither tribe, which made it a neutral capital for a king of all Israel. Its old name was Salem, Melchizedek's city (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2).
r: Judges 1:21; Joshua 15:63; Judges 19:10–12; Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2; 1 Chronicles 11:4–5

a: The blind and the lame will turn you back
p: A taunt, a curse ritual, or something else? The phrase is one of the hardest in the book.
b: The simplest reading: the walls are so strong that blind and lame men could hold them. Josephus says the Jebusites put the blind and the lame on the walls to mock David (Antiquities 7.3.1). Yigael Yadin compared a Hittite soldiers' oath, in which a blind woman and a deaf man were shown to the troops as a warning of what would happen to oath-breakers; the defenders may have performed such a curse. A midrash cited by Rashi says the "blind and lame" were images of Isaac and Jacob, guarding a treaty Abraham had made with the Jebusites. David then turns the Jebusites' phrase back on them (5:8).

a: Zion's fortress
p: The first mention of Zion in the Bible: the fortified hill of the Jebusite city.
b: "Zion" first names the Jebusite citadel on the narrow ridge south of the later temple mount, above the Gihon spring. It becomes the name of the temple hill and of Jerusalem itself (Psalm 2:6; Isaiah 2:3). Excavations on this ridge, the "City of David," have found a massive Stepped Stone Structure and, above it, the Large Stone Structure that Eilat Mazar identified in 2005 as David's palace. Dating both is debated: some archaeologists place them in the 10th century BC, others earlier or later.

a: the water shaft
p: Hebrew tsinnor appears only here and in Psalm 42:7. Its meaning is uncertain.
b: Tsinnor means something like a channel or conduit (Psalm 42:7, "your waterfalls"). Since the 1800s many have linked it to Warren's Shaft, a vertical shaft discovered by Charles Warren in 1867 that reaches the Gihon spring, imagining Joab climbing up it. Excavations by Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron in the 1990s showed that the shaft was probably not open in the Bronze Age, though a fortified tower guarded the spring. Others take tsinnor as a gutter, a grappling hook, or even the "windpipe" ("go for the throat"). Chronicles leaves it out and says the first to strike would become commander, and Joab went up first (1 Chronicles 11:6).

a: No one blind or lame may come into the house
t: The blind and the lame in the house
p: A saying that kept the disabled out of "the house." Jesus welcomes them into the temple.
b: The saying is tied to the Jebusites' taunt, but its sense is debated. "The house" may be the palace or the temple. Israel's law already barred priests with defects from serving at the altar: "No man with a defect may come near: no man who is blind or lame" (Leviticus 21:18). A Dead Sea scroll (the Rule of the Congregation, 1QSa) shuts the lame and blind out of the end-time assembly. Matthew records that "blind and lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them" (Matthew 21:14), and Jesus tells his host to invite the crippled, the lame and the blind (Luke 14:13, 14:21). In this book, David himself brings lame Mephibosheth to his table (9:13). The phrase "the ones David's soul hates" follows the Hebrew reading tradition; see the variant.

a: the Millo
p: The name means "filling." It was probably an earthwork or terraced platform.
b: Millo comes from male', "to fill." It seems to have been a fill of earth and stone that supported buildings on the steep slope. Solomon later "built the Millo" (1 Kings 9:15, 9:24) and Hezekiah strengthened it (2 Chronicles 32:5). Some archaeologists identify it with the Stepped Stone Structure on the east slope of the City of David. There was also a "Beth-millo" at Shechem (Judges 9:6).

a: the LORD, the God of Armies
p: Hebrew YHWH tseva'ot: "armies" may be Israel's armies, angels, or the stars.
b: Tseva'ot is the plural of tsava', "army, host." This translation renders the title "the LORD of Armies" in every book. The armies may be Israel's (1 Samuel 17:45), the angels (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 103:20–21), or the stars (Isaiah 40:26); the title probably includes them all. It is closely tied to the ark, "the LORD of Armies, who sits on the cherubim" (6:2; 1 Samuel 4:4). Here the Masoretic Text says "the LORD, the God of Armies"; the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a reads just "the LORD of Armies," as in 6:2.

a: Hiram, king of Tyre
p: Tyre was the great Phoenician port. Its cedar and craftsmen also built Solomon's temple.
b: Tyre, on an island off the Lebanese coast, controlled the timber of the Lebanon mountains. Hiram later sends cedar and builders to Solomon (1 Kings 5:1–12). Josephus, quoting Phoenician records, places the temple's building in Hiram's twelfth year (Against Apion 1.126), which makes it hard for the same Hiram to have built David's house early in his reign. So either Hiram's gift came late in David's reign, or the narrator has grouped events by subject, not by date. Chapters 5–8 often do this.

a: for the good of his people Israel
t: A kingdom for the people's sake
p: David understands that God raised his kingdom for Israel's sake, not his own.
b: Deuteronomy's law of the king forbids him to think himself above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:20). Here David knows that his rise is "for the sake of his people." The next verse, about more wives and concubines, puts a question mark beside that knowledge. Commentators often note how the book sets David's best moments next to signs of the trouble to come.

a: he took still more wives and concubines
p: Deuteronomy's law said, "He must not take many wives for himself."
b: The law of the king said, "He must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside" (Deuteronomy 17:17). Royal marriages sealed alliances and showed power, and David's harem grows as his kingdom does. The narrator does not comment, but the next chapters show what comes of a large royal family: rival sons, rape and murder (chapters 13–18). Ten of these concubines will be left to keep the palace when David flees (15:16).

a: Nathan, Solomon
t: Nathan and Solomon in the genealogies of Jesus
p: Matthew traces Jesus through Solomon, Luke through Nathan.
b: Both were sons of Bathsheba (called Bath-shua in 1 Chronicles 3:5). Matthew's genealogy runs through Solomon and the kings of Judah (Matthew 1:6–7); Luke's runs through Nathan (Luke 3:31). Christians have explained the difference in several ways: one list follows Joseph's legal line and the other Mary's, or one follows royal succession and the other physical descent. This Nathan is not Nathan the prophet (7:2).

a: Eliada
p: Chronicles once calls this son Beeliada, "Baal knows." Another changed baal name.
b: In 1 Chronicles 14:7 the name is Beeliada, "Baal knows"; here and in 1 Chronicles 3:8 it is Eliada, "God knows." As with Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth (2:8; 4:4), a name with baal in it seems to have been changed by later scribes. It shows that in David's day baal, "lord," could still be used in Israelite names, probably of the LORD.

a: went down to the stronghold
p: "Went down" suggests the cave of Adullam, not the hilltop of Zion.
b: One goes "up" to Jerusalem, so "went down to the stronghold" probably means a refuge in the lowlands, such as Adullam, where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1–4; 23:13–14). That suggests that these Philistine wars came soon after David was made king of Israel, perhaps before he took Jerusalem. The narrator has grouped David's victories by theme. The Philistines had seen David as their vassal while he lived at Ziklag (1 Samuel 27); his anointing over all Israel ended that.

a: the Valley of Rephaim
p: A broad valley southwest of Jerusalem, on the road from Philistia. The name recalls ancient giants.
b: The valley lay on the border between Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:8; 18:16), a natural route into the hills from the coast. The Rephaim were an old people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11), and in poetry the word means the shades of the dead (Isaiah 14:9). The Philistines camp there again in 23:13.

a: Baal-perazim
p: The place name plays on the verb parats, "burst out." Isaiah remembers this battle.
b: Baal means "lord" and perazim "breakthroughs." David says the LORD "burst through" his enemies like floodwater breaking a dam, so the place is "Lord of breakthroughs," here a name for the LORD, not for the god Baal. The same verb names Perez, Judah's son who "burst out" first (Genesis 38:29), and Perez-uzzah, where the LORD bursts out against Uzzah (6:8). Isaiah warns that the LORD will rise "as at Mount Perazim," but this time against his own people (Isaiah 28:21).

a: There the Philistines left their idols behind
p: The Philistines once carried off Israel's ark. Now Israel carries off the Philistines' gods.
b: Armies took their gods into battle, and victors carried off the enemy's images (Isaiah 46:1–2; Jeremiah 48:7). The Philistines had once captured the ark (1 Samuel 4:11) and set it beside Dagon (1 Samuel 5:2). Now the reverse happens. Chronicles adds that David ordered the images burned (1 Chronicles 14:12), as Deuteronomy commanded (Deuteronomy 7:5, 7:25); here the text says only that David's men took them away.
r: 1 Samuel 4:11; 1 Samuel 5:1–5; 1 Chronicles 14:12; Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 7:25; Isaiah 46:1–2

a: the baka trees
p: No one knows what tree bekha'im were: balsam, mulberry, poplar and others have been suggested.
b: Bakha' may come from a root meaning "to weep," suggesting a tree that drips sap, such as a balsam. The King James Version has "mulberry trees"; others suggest poplars or a kind of shrub. The "valley of Baca" in Psalm 84:6 may be named for the same plant. The Plain keeps the Hebrew name, since the identification is a guess.

a: something like marching in the treetops
t: The sound of an army in the trees
p: The rustling in the treetops is the LORD's army moving ahead of David.
b: God tells David to wait for a sign: a sound of marching overhead. The LORD himself goes out before Israel's army, as in the songs of the exodus and of Deborah (Judges 4:14; Judges 5:4). The idea of heavenly troops fighting for Israel appears again when the Arameans hear the sound of chariots and horses (2 Kings 7:6) and Elisha's servant sees the hills full of fire (2 Kings 6:17). This is the "LORD of Armies" in action (5:10).
r: Judges 4:14; Judges 5:4; Judges 5:20; 2 Kings 6:17; 2 Kings 7:6; 1 Chronicles 14:15

a: all the way to where you enter Gezer
p: Gezer guarded the road from the coast into the hills. David pushed the Philistines back to their own plain.
b: Gezer stood where the hill country meets the coastal plain. It stayed Canaanite until a pharaoh captured it and gave it to Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). David's victory drives the Philistines out of the hills for good; they will never again threaten Israel's heartland in this book. On whether the pursuit began at Geba or at Gibeon, see the variant.

a: thirty thousand
p: Israel's picked men gather to escort the ark. The Greek text says seventy thousand.
b: "Picked men" usually means soldiers (1 Samuel 24:2). The ark had once been taken from Israel's army by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:10–11), and David brings an army to escort it. The Greek translators read seventy thousand (see the variant). Chronicles turns the event into a gathering of all Israel, "from the Shihor of Egypt to Lebo-hamath," with priests and Levites (1 Chronicles 13:1–5).

a: who sits on the cherubim as his throne
p: The ark was God's throne, or his footstool, with the winged cherubim forming the seat.
b: Two golden cherubim faced each other on the ark's lid, with wings spread (Exodus 25:18–22). Ancient kings sat on thrones flanked by winged creatures, like the winged-sphinx throne carved on the stone coffin of Ahiram of Byblos and the ivory carvings of a king on such a throne found at Megiddo. So the empty space above the ark was the LORD's seat; the ark itself was his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:1, 99:5). The ark had sat neglected in Kiriath-jearim for some twenty years and more (1 Samuel 7:1–2). David brings God's throne to his capital.
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1; Psalm 99:5; 1 Chronicles 28:2; 2 Kings 19:15

a: which is called by the Name
p: The Hebrew repeats "name": "called by the name, the name of the LORD of Armies."
b: The Hebrew says "called by name, the name of the LORD of Armies." The first "name" may be a copying slip, or it may be a solemn way of saying the ark is where the LORD's own Name is invoked. In Deuteronomy God sets his Name at the place he chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5, 12:11), and later Jewish tradition used "the Name" (hashem) in place of saying YHWH. The ark carries that Name into Jerusalem, which becomes the place God chooses (1 Kings 8:29).
orig: נִקְרָא שֵׁם שֵׁם יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (niqra shem shem YHWH tseva'ot)

a: onto a new cart
t: A new cart, the Philistine way
p: The Philistines sent the ark home on a new cart. God's law said Levites must carry it on poles.
b: The Philistines had returned the ark on a new cart pulled by cows (1 Samuel 6:7–8). David copies them. But the law said the ark was to be carried on poles by the Levites of Kohath (Exodus 25:14; Numbers 7:9), who "must not touch the holy things. If they do, they will die" (Numbers 4:15). When David tries again, Chronicles says, he has the Levites carry it, explaining that the LORD broke out against them the first time because "we did not seek him the way the ruling requires" (1 Chronicles 15:13–15). The new cart was well meant, but it was the wrong way.
r: 1 Samuel 6:7–8; Exodus 25:14; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9; 1 Chronicles 15:2; 1 Chronicles 15:13–15; 6:13

a: the house of Abinadab up on the hill
p: The ark had stayed at Kiriath-jearim since the Philistines sent it back.
b: After the disaster at Beth-shemesh the ark was taken "into the house of Abinadab on the hill," and his son Eleazar was set apart to guard it (1 Samuel 7:1). It stayed there through Saul's reign; Saul does not seem to have consulted it (1 Chronicles 13:3). Uzzah and Ahio were Abinadab's "sons," perhaps grandsons. "The hill" (haggiv'ah) can also be read as the name Gibeah.

a: with lyres, harps, hand drums, rattles and cymbals
p: String, drum and rattle: a joyful festival band.
b: The kinnor was a small lyre, David's instrument (1 Samuel 16:23); the nevel was a larger harp or lyre; the tof a hand drum, often played by women (Exodus 15:20); the mena'an'im (only here) were probably sistrums, rattles shaken on a handle, known from Egypt; and the tseltselim were cymbals. Chronicles adds trumpets and singers (1 Chronicles 13:8; 1 Chronicles 15:16–28). On "with all their strength and with songs," see the variant.

a: the oxen stumbled
p: The verb may mean the oxen stumbled, slipped, or shook the cart.
b: Shamat usually means "to let drop, let go" (as in the year of release, Deuteronomy 15:2). Here it may mean that the oxen stumbled or let the cart tip, so the ark seemed about to fall. Chronicles uses the same word (1 Chronicles 13:9). Threshing floors were flat, hard places, so the jolt may have come on the way up to it.

a: The LORD's anger burned against Uzzah
p: Uzzah reached out to steady the ark and died. Readers have long found this hard.
b: The holiness reading: the ark was the place of God's presence, and the law said that even the Levites who carried it must not touch it or they would die (Numbers 4:15, 4:20). The fault was not only Uzzah's: the whole procession ignored the law (6:3), and Chronicles says so (1 Chronicles 15:13). The rabbis said that David was punished for treating the commandments lightly; one tradition says it was because he called God's laws "songs" (Psalm 119:54), so forgot what was written about carrying the ark (Bavli Sotah 35a). The same passage says that the ark carried its bearers, so Uzzah's grab showed that he did not trust it to keep itself from falling. Critical scholars often read the episode as part of an old ark narrative (Leonhard Rost), and the story as explaining the place name Perez-uzzah, "Uzzah's Breakout" (6:8). The Hebrew says God struck him "for the shal," a word found only here; the Greek gives no reason at all, and Chronicles says it was because he put out his hand (see the variant). Many modern readers, including some evangelicals and critics such as Eric Seibert, find the story troubling, since Uzzah meant well. The text itself does not explain beyond "the LORD's anger burned." David's own response is anger and fear (6:8–9).
r: Numbers 4:15; Numbers 4:20; 1 Samuel 6:19; Leviticus 10:1–3; 1 Chronicles 13:9–12; 1 Chronicles 15:13

a: It made David angry
p: The Hebrew says "it burned to David." It can mean anger or deep distress.
b: The same verb was just used of the LORD's anger (6:7). "It burned to David" usually means he was angry (1 Samuel 15:11, where Samuel is upset). Some translate "David was upset" or "grieved." The play on words continues: the LORD "burst out" a "breakout" (parats perets) against Uzzah, as he had burst through David's enemies at Baal-perazim (5:20). The God who broke out for David now breaks out against his procession.

a: Obed-edom the Gittite
p: "Gittite" usually means from Gath. Chronicles makes him a Levite musician and gatekeeper.
b: "The Gittite" normally means a man from the Philistine city of Gath, like Ittai the Gittite (15:19). If so, David left the ark with a foreigner, perhaps one of his men from his years in Gath (1 Samuel 27:2–3). Chronicles lists an Obed-edom among the Levite gatekeepers and musicians (1 Chronicles 15:18, 15:24; 1 Chronicles 16:5; 1 Chronicles 26:4–8), and some think he came from Gath-rimmon, a Levite town (Joshua 21:24). His name means "servant of Edom," perhaps a divine name. Whoever he was, the ark blessed his house.

a: the LORD has blessed Obed-edom's family
p: The ark brought plague to the Philistines and death to Uzzah, but blessing to Obed-edom.
b: Wherever the ark went in the Philistine cities, tumors and panic followed (1 Samuel 5:6–12). At Beth-shemesh men died for looking into it (1 Samuel 6:19). Now it brings blessing. Chronicles says Obed-edom's family had many sons (1 Chronicles 26:4–5). The lesson David draws is that God's presence is a blessing when it is received rightly, and he tries again.

a: The bearers of the LORD's ark took six steps
p: Did David sacrifice once, after six steps, or every six steps?
b: This time the ark is carried, not carted (6:3). Most readers think David sacrificed once, after the bearers had taken six steps safely, as a thank-offering that God accepted the move. Another view is that he sacrificed every six steps along the whole way; the Talmud records a debate between the two readings (Bavli Sotah 35b). The witnesses differ on what was offered. The Greek has "seven dancing groups" with the ark and "a calf and lambs" as the sacrifice, and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a is reported (Ulrich; DJD 17) to have seven bulls and seven rams, like 1 Chronicles 15:26. See the variant.

a: a linen ephod
p: A short priestly garment. David leads worship like a priest.
b: The linen ephod was worn by priests (1 Samuel 22:18) and by the boy Samuel serving at Shiloh (1 Samuel 2:18). It was probably a short apron or kilt, which explains Michal's complaint (6:20). David wears it, offers sacrifices (6:17) and blesses the people (6:18), acting as a priest-king. Psalm 110:4 makes the king of David's line a priest for all time, in the line of Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem (Genesis 14:18). See also David's sons as priests (8:18).

a: David whirled before the LORD
p: Two rare verbs describe David's dance: whirling (karar) and leaping (pazaz).
b: Mekharker occurs only in this chapter and seems to mean spinning or whirling. In 6:16 he is "leaping" (mefazzez, found only there) and "whirling." Chronicles replaces them with "dancing and celebrating" (1 Chronicles 15:29). Dance was part of Israel's worship and victory celebrations (Exodus 15:20; Judges 11:34; Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4). David dances "with all his strength," giving himself to it without concern for dignity.

a: shouting and blowing the ram's horn
p: Psalms that celebrate God going up to Zion may remember this procession.
b: The teru'ah is the war cry or festal shout, and the shofar the ram's horn. Psalm 47:5 pictures God going up amid shouts and the blast of the horn, and Psalm 24:7–10 calls the gates to open for the King of glory, the LORD of Armies. Psalm 132 asks God to arise to his resting place with the ark of his might (Psalm 132:8). Jewish and Christian interpreters have long linked these psalms with David's procession, though the psalms themselves do not say so.

a: looked down from the window
p: Michal once helped David escape through a window. Now she watches him from one with contempt.
b: Years before, "Michal lowered David through the window" to save him from her father (1 Samuel 19:12). Now she looks down on him through a window. A woman at a window is a recurring image in the Bible, often of someone cut off from the action: Sisera's mother waiting in vain (Judges 5:28), Jezebel before her death (2 Kings 9:30). The narrator calls her "Saul's daughter," not "David's wife," three times (6:16, 6:20, 6:23).

a: the tent that David had set up for it
p: David housed the ark in a new tent. The old tabernacle stood at Gibeon, according to Chronicles.
b: Chronicles says that the tabernacle Moses made and the bronze altar remained at the high place of Gibeon, where Zadok served (1 Chronicles 16:39; 1 Chronicles 21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3–5). The ark stayed in David's tent in Jerusalem until Solomon brought it into the temple (1 Kings 8:1–6). So for a generation Israel had two centers of worship. David's tent becomes the subject of chapter 7: the king lives in cedar, the ark in curtains (7:2).

a: he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Armies
p: Blessing in God's name was the priests' task, yet David and Solomon both do it.
b: The priests were told to bless Israel in the LORD's name (Numbers 6:23–27; Deuteronomy 10:8). Here and at the temple's dedication the king does it (1 Kings 8:14, 8:55). Melchizedek, priest and king of Salem, blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:19). Whether David took a priestly role or simply spoke a royal blessing is debated.
r: Numbers 6:23–27; Deuteronomy 10:8; 1 Kings 8:14; 1 Kings 8:55; Genesis 14:19; 1 Chronicles 16:2

a: one date cake
t: A date cake or a portion of meat?
p: The word eshpar occurs only here and in Chronicles. Its meaning is a guess.
b: Each person received bread, a cake of raisins, and an eshpar. The Latin Vulgate and the King James Version took it as a portion of meat ("a good piece of flesh"), fitting the sacrifices just offered. Others link it to a word for dates, hence "date cake," which pairs well with the raisin cake. Raisin cakes were festival food (Hosea 3:1; Song of Songs 2:5). The meal is a festival for everyone, "man and woman alike."

a: What honor the king of Israel won today!
p: Michal mocks David's "honor." David answers that he will be honored by those she scorns.
b: The root kaved, "to be heavy, honored," frames the quarrel. Michal says sarcastically, "How honored the king of Israel was today," and David replies that he will be "honored" by the slave girls (6:22). She thinks a king's dignity lies in keeping himself apart; he thinks it lies in humbling himself before God. Her word "stripped" suggests that his short ephod showed too much as he danced (compare Exodus 20:26). Her insult, "one of the empty ones" (hareqim), is the word for the idle, reckless men who followed Abimelech and Jephthah (Judges 9:4; Judges 11:3). It is a different word from beliyya'al, "worthless," used of Nabal and of David's troublemakers (1 Samuel 25:25; 1 Samuel 30:22).
orig: מַה־נִּכְבַּד הַיּוֹם מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל (mah-nikhbad hayyom melekh Yisra'el)

a: He chose me instead of your father
p: David's reply is sharp: God chose him over Michal's father and family.
b: David reminds Michal that God passed over Saul's house for him. The cut is deliberate, and many readers see in it the end of the marriage. Jewish tradition generally sides with David: Michal despised the joy of worship. Some modern readers sympathize with Michal, a woman passed between husbands (3:14–16) who now sees David humiliate her father's memory. Both see that the scene marks the end of Saul's line as a royal line: the last word about Saul's daughter is that she bore no child (6:23).

a: had no child until the day she died
p: Was it God's judgment, David's choice, or Michal's? The text does not say.
b: The verse states a fact, not a cause. Some readers see God's judgment on Michal's contempt. Others think David never came to her again. Others stress the political meaning: no son of Saul's daughter will ever sit on David's throne. The Talmud identifies Michal with Eglah, the mother of Ithream (3:5), and says she had a child on the day she died (Bavli Sanhedrin 21a). In 21:8 the Masoretic Text speaks of "the five sons of Michal"; most think Merab is meant there (see the note there).

a: the LORD had let him rest from every enemy around him
t: Rest, then a house for God
p: Deuteronomy said that when God gave rest from enemies, Israel would worship at the place he chose.
b: Moses promised that when the LORD gave Israel rest from all its enemies around, they would bring their offerings to the place he would choose for his name (Deuteronomy 12:10–11). David has rest, the ark is in Jerusalem, and so he thinks of a temple. Yet 7:11 promises rest still to come, and the wars of chapters 8 and 10 have not been fought yet. The chapter is probably placed here by theme, not by date. Solomon later says David could not build because of his wars, until God gave rest (1 Kings 5:3–4).

a: I live in a house made of cedar
p: The whole chapter plays on bayit: David's palace, God's temple, and David's royal line.
b: David contrasts his cedar house with God's tent. God answers that David will not build him a house (temple, 7:5); God will make David a house (dynasty, 7:11); David's son will build a house for God's name (7:13); and David's house will stand forever (7:16). The word comes fifteen times in the chapter. The play on one word turns a building project into a promise about a family that will last.

a: Nathan the prophet
p: Nathan appears here for the first time. He will confront David in chapter 12.
b: Nathan has no introduction, no father's name and no hometown. He is simply "the prophet" at David's court, one of the first court prophets in Israel. He brings God's promise here, God's judgment after Bathsheba (12:1–15), and later secures Solomon's succession (1 Kings 1). Chronicles credits him with a written history of David and Solomon (1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29).

a: Whatever is in your heart, go and do it
p: Nathan approves David's plan, then God overrules him that same night.
b: Nathan's first answer is his own opinion, the natural reply to a king with good intentions. That night God sends another message. Jewish and Christian interpreters have drawn the lesson that a prophet speaks for God only when God speaks, and that his own advice can be wrong (compare 1 Kings 13:18; Jeremiah 28:5–9). Some modern readers see politics in the story: priests or prophets who opposed a temple, or a later writer explaining why David did not build one.

a: Is it you who will build a house for me to live in?
p: Samuel says God never asked for a house. Chronicles adds that David had shed too much blood.
b: Here God's reason is that he has never lived in a house and never asked for one (7:6–7); and the son, not David, will build (7:13). Chronicles gives another reason: David had shed much blood and fought great wars (1 Chronicles 22:8; 1 Chronicles 28:3). 1 Kings says he was too busy with war (1 Kings 5:3). The question "Is it you?" stresses the word "you": God will do the building. Some see here a strand in Israel wary of temples, heard again in Isaiah 66:1 and in Stephen's speech, which quotes it (Acts 7:47–50).
r: 7:6–7; 7:13; 1 Chronicles 22:8; 1 Chronicles 28:3; 1 Kings 5:3; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:47–50; 1 Chronicles 17:4

a: in a tent, in a tabernacle
p: Ohel and mishkan, the two names of the wilderness sanctuary.
b: This translation renders ohel "tent" and mishkan "tabernacle," the dwelling of Exodus 25–40. God says he has always moved with his people. Readers have noted that the sanctuary at Shiloh is called a "house" or "temple" in 1 Samuel 1:9, 1:24 and 3:3, with doors and doorposts. Most explain that the Shiloh shrine was a more solid building around the tent, or that God's point is that he never commanded a permanent house of cedar (7:7).

a: from walking behind the flock
p: God took David from the sheep, as he later took Amos.
b: David was out with the sheep when Samuel came to anoint him (1 Samuel 16:11). Psalm 78:70–72 sings of God choosing David and taking him from the sheepfolds to shepherd Jacob. The prophet Amos uses nearly the same words of his own call: the LORD took him "from following the flock" (Amos 7:15). God's choices in Samuel keep raising the low (1 Samuel 2:7–8).

a: a name as great as the names of the great men on the earth
p: God promises David what he promised Abraham. The builders of Babel tried to make one for themselves.
b: God told Abraham, "I will bless you and make your name great" (Genesis 12:2). The builders of Babel wanted to "make a name" for themselves (Genesis 11:4). Here, as with Abraham, the great name is God's gift. In 8:13 David "won fame," literally "made a name." Many scholars see God's promise to David as a renewal of the promise to Abraham, now focused on one royal family.

a: I will pick out a place for my people
p: The "place" may be the land, or the temple site God chooses.
b: Maqom, "place," can mean land or a holy site; Deuteronomy speaks of "the place the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5). Some read 7:10 as a promise of secure land; others as a promise of the sanctuary where Israel will be "planted," as in the Song of the Sea: "You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain that is your own" (Exodus 15:17). The verbs are in the future, though the land was already Israel's, so the promise is of security, not first possession.
r: Deuteronomy 12:5; Exodus 15:17; Psalm 44:2; Psalm 80:8; Jeremiah 24:6; Amos 9:15

a: the LORD will make a house for you
t: God will make David a house
p: The turning point of the chapter: David wanted to build God a house; God will build David's.
