b: Here "house" means a dynasty, a royal family line. The reversal is the heart of the chapter: David will not build for God; God will build for David. Jewish tradition and Christian theology both treat the promise as the root of the hope for a Messiah, son of David. Notice the sudden change from first person ("I will give you rest") to the third person ("the LORD tells you"), which gives the promise the weight of a formal announcement.

a: your offspring
p: The word means "seed": one descendant or a whole line. Here the pronouns are singular.
b: Zera', "seed," can mean one child or all one's descendants. In 7:12–15 the pronouns are singular ("his kingdom," "he will build"), and 1 Kings applies them to Solomon (1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:19–20). Yet the promise reaches "for all time," beyond any one king. Jewish readers have seen the line of David leading to the Messiah; Christian readers, from the New Testament on, see Jesus as the offspring (Acts 13:23; Romans 1:3; compare Paul's argument about Abraham's singular offspring in Galatians 3:16).
r: 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:19–20; Acts 13:23; Romans 1:3; Galatians 3:16; Genesis 15:4; Psalm 132:11

a: He will build a house for my name
p: Solomon built the temple, and he quoted this promise when he did.
b: Solomon tells Hiram he will build a house for the LORD's name as God promised David (1 Kings 5:5), and at the dedication he says God has kept his word (1 Kings 8:15–20). Chronicles makes the link to Solomon explicit (1 Chronicles 22:9–10). Christian readers also see a further meaning: Jesus speaks of the temple of his body (John 2:19–21), and the church is called God's house (1 Corinthians 3:16; Hebrews 3:6). Zechariah's "Branch" will build the LORD's temple (Zechariah 6:12–13).
r: 1 Kings 5:5; 1 Kings 8:15–20; 1 Chronicles 22:9–10; Zechariah 6:12–13; John 2:19–21; Hebrews 3:6

a: for all time
p: Was the promise unconditional? The word means lasting, and the later history tested it.
b: 'Ad-'olam means "forever, for all time," a time without a set end. The words come eight times in this chapter. Elsewhere David's heirs are told the throne depends on obedience (1 Kings 2:4; 1 Kings 9:4–7; Psalm 132:12), while 7:14–15 says sin will be punished but loyal love will not be withdrawn. When Babylon ended the dynasty in 586 BC, Psalm 89 held God to his oath (Psalm 89:38–51). Jews hoped for the restoring of David's line; Christians read the promise as kept in Jesus, whose reign "will have no end" (Luke 1:33).

a: I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me
p: The king as God's son: quoted in Hebrews of Jesus, and adapted by Paul for believers.
b: Ancient kings were often called sons of their gods. In Israel the language is adoption: God takes the king as his son (Psalm 2:7; Psalm 89:26–27). A Dead Sea scroll, the Florilegium (4Q174), quotes 7:10–14 and explains the son as "the Branch of David" of the last days. Hebrews 1:5 sets this verse beside Psalm 2:7 to show that the Son is greater than the angels. Paul adapts it for all God's people, changing "son" to "sons and daughters" (2 Corinthians 6:18).
r: Psalm 2:7; Psalm 89:26–27; Hebrews 1:5; 2 Corinthians 6:18; Revelation 21:7; 1 Chronicles 17:13

a: If he does wrong, I will correct him
p: The promise expects the son to sin. Chronicles leaves the line out.
b: God will discipline David's son as a father does, "with a rod such as men use," but not reject him. Solomon and many later kings sinned, and the books of Kings tell their punishment. 1 Chronicles 17:13 omits this clause, perhaps because the Chronicler looked ahead to the ideal king. For Christians who apply 7:14 to Jesus, the clause raises a question; most answer that the promise was first fulfilled in Solomon and the kings, and fulfilled fully in Christ, who bore punishment for others' wrongs (Isaiah 53:5). Classical Jewish commentators, such as Rashi and Radak, read 7:12–15 first of Solomon, who built the temple and whose sins were punished. Jewish writers answering Christian claims have pointed to this very clause: a son who can do wrong cannot be the sinless Son of Christian teaching, so the promise is about the kings of David's line. Jewish readers see a realistic promise: David's line will be chastened but never abandoned, and the Messiah will come from it.
r: 1 Kings 11:9–13; 1 Kings 11:31–39; Psalm 89:30–34; 1 Chronicles 17:13; Isaiah 53:5; Hebrews 12:5–7

a: But my loyal love will not turn away from him
p: God's promise resembles grants that ancient kings gave loyal servants, land or dynasty forever.
b: Moshe Weinfeld compared God's promises to Abraham and David with ancient "covenants of grant," in which a king rewarded a faithful servant with land or a lasting house. Unlike a vassal treaty, which bound the servant, a grant bound the giver, and the gift could not be taken back, though a disloyal heir might be punished. Hittite and Babylonian texts use phrases close to this verse. Saul's case is the contrast: God took his loyal love from Saul (1 Samuel 15:28), but he will not take it from David's house.

a: Your house and your kingdom will be made secure forever
t: How the promise has been read
p: Jews and Christians both build their hope of a Messiah on this verse, in different ways.
b: Jewish tradition holds that the promise is still in force: the Messiah will be a descendant of David, and the daily Amidah prays for the "sprout of David" to flourish. The New Testament announces Jesus as the son of David who receives "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30). Critical scholars often see the oracle as royal propaganda from David's or Solomon's court, later reread in the exile as a hope; some see the conditional verses (1 Kings 2:4) as a later answer to the dynasty's fall. All agree that no single verse did more to shape the hope for a Messiah.
r: Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30; Psalm 89:3–4; Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 33:17; Amos 9:11; 1 Kings 2:4

a: the whole of this vision
p: God spoke to Nathan by night, in what the text calls a vision.
b: Chizzayon is a word for a revelation, often at night (Job 4:13; Job 33:15). The word came to Nathan "that night" (7:4). Psalm 89:19 refers back to it: God once spoke in a vision to his faithful ones and said he had set the crown on a warrior chosen from the people.

a: King David went in and sat down before the LORD
p: David prays sitting, perhaps before the ark in its tent.
b: People usually stood or knelt to pray (1 Kings 8:22, 8:54). David "went in," probably into the tent where the ark stood (6:17), and sat. The Talmud uses this verse for the rule that no one might sit in the temple court except kings of David's line (Bavli Yoma 25a). The prayer that follows is humble and bold together: "Who am I?" and then "Do just what you said" (7:25).

a: Lord GOD
p: Adonai YHWH, "the Lord YHWH," is printed "Lord GOD" to avoid writing "Lord LORD."
b: When Adonai ("Lord") stands beside the divine name YHWH, Jewish readers say Adonai Elohim, and English Bibles print "Lord GOD." David uses the double title seven times in this prayer (7:18, 7:19 twice, 7:20, 7:22, 7:28, 7:29), more than anywhere else in Samuel. It shows his sense of speaking to his master: he calls himself "your servant" ten times.

a: And this is the law for humankind, Lord GOD!
p: One of the hardest phrases in Samuel. Torat ha'adam may mean "the way of people," "a charter for humanity," or something else.
b: Literally: "and this is the torah of the man (or of humankind)." (1) A question: "Is this the way you deal with a mere man?" (2) The way people act: the King James Version, "is this the manner of man?" (3) A charter for humanity: Walter Kaiser argued that the promise to David is God's plan for all people, a reading some evangelicals follow. (4) Chronicles has a different text: "you have seen me as one would see a man of high rank" (1 Chronicles 17:17). Many scholars think the Hebrew here is damaged. The Plain gives torah its usual rendering, "law," and the reader may hear "teaching" in it.

a: because of your word
p: Chronicles reads "for your servant's sake." The two Hebrew words look alike.
b: Samuel has devarkha, "your word"; 1 Chronicles 17:19 has avdekha, "your servant." The two look similar in Hebrew script. Either way, David traces God's great deed to God's own will, "because your heart wanted it," not to David's merit. Some, following the Greek, read "your servant" here too.

a: No God exists except you
p: David's prayer echoes Hannah's song and Moses' words.
b: Hannah sang that there is no one holy like the LORD and no one besides him (1 Samuel 2:2). Moses told Israel that the LORD is God and there is no other (Deuteronomy 4:35, 4:39). "Everything we have heard with our ears" points to the story of the exodus, which David summarizes next (7:23).

a: God went to redeem them
p: In Hebrew the verb "went" is plural here. Chronicles makes it singular.
b: Elohim is plural in form, but used of Israel's God it normally takes singular verbs. Here the verb is plural (halekhu), as if "gods went." Chronicles has the singular (1 Chronicles 17:21). The Talmud lists this verse among those that heretics used to argue for many gods, and answers that the next words, "for himself," show one God (Bavli Sanhedrin 38b). Some Christian writers saw a hint of the Trinity; most scholars see a grammatical slip or a scribe treating Elohim as plural.

a: opened your servant's ear
p: A Hebrew idiom for revealing something to someone.
b: To "uncover someone's ear" is to tell him a secret or reveal something (1 Samuel 9:15; 1 Samuel 20:2; Ruth 4:4). God revealed to David what he never could have asked for. "Found it in his heart" means found the courage. The prayer moves from "Who am I?" to bold petition, because God has spoken first.

a: Metheg-ammah
p: A puzzle. It may be a place name, or a phrase meaning "control of the capital."
b: Meteg ha'ammah could mean "the bridle of the forearm" or "the bridle of the mother city," that is, control over Gath, the leading Philistine city. Chronicles reads "Gath and its villages" (1 Chronicles 18:1), which supports that idea. Others think it is an unknown place. The general sense is clear: David took control from the Philistines.

a: measured them with a cord
p: Two-thirds of the Moabite prisoners were put to death. Why, when David had Moabite ancestry and friends?
b: David's great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabite (Ruth 4:17), and he had left his parents with the king of Moab for safety (1 Samuel 22:3–4). So the harshness surprises. The text gives no reason. A rabbinic midrash says the king of Moab had killed David's parents (Numbers Rabbah 14:1). Others see ordinary ancient warfare, or the fulfillment of Balaam's oracle against Moab: "It will smash the brows of Moab" (Numbers 24:17). Some readers simply note that the narrator reports it without praise. Moab becomes a tributary state until it rebels after Ahab (2 Kings 3:4–5).
r: Ruth 4:17; 1 Samuel 22:3–4; Numbers 24:17; 2 Kings 3:4–5; 1 Chronicles 18:2; Psalm 60:8

a: as he was on his way to take back his control at the Euphrates River
p: "He went" could be Hadadezer or David. "His hand" means power, or perhaps a monument.
b: The Hebrew does not say whose journey it was. Most think Hadadezer was marching to restore his control in the north, toward the Euphrates, when David struck his kingdom from behind. Others think David was the one going to set up his power there, fulfilling the old promise of the land as far as the great river (Genesis 15:18; Deuteronomy 11:24). "Hand" can mean a victory monument (1 Samuel 15:12), so some read "to set up his stele." Zobah was an Aramean kingdom north of Damascus in the Beqaa Valley.

a: by cutting their leg tendons
p: David crippled the captured chariot horses, as Joshua had done.
b: Joshua was told to hamstring the horses of the northern kings and burn their chariots (Joshua 11:6, 11:9). Cutting the tendon above the hock made a horse useless for war. The law of the king warned that "he must not get himself many horses" (Deuteronomy 17:16). David kept enough for a hundred chariots; Solomon would build up thousands (1 Kings 10:26). Israel's trust was to be in God, not horses (Psalm 20:7).

a: Everywhere David went, the LORD made him win
p: The verb is yasha', "save, give victory." The line comes twice and frames the war list.
b: Literally "the LORD saved David wherever he went." The refrain comes at 8:6 and 8:14, around the Aramean and Edomite campaigns, and credits every victory to God. Victory and salvation are the same word in Hebrew; the name Joshua (and Jesus) comes from it.

a: The gold shields
p: Hebrew shelet appears only a few times. It may mean shield, quiver or armor.
b: Shelet is used of warriors' gear hung on a tower (Song of Songs 4:4; Ezekiel 27:11) and is paired with arrows in Jeremiah 51:11. Many translate "shields"; others "quivers" or "bow cases." Gold ones would be ceremonial, carried by the king's officers. David later gave such shields to the temple (2 Kings 11:10). On the Greek and Dead Sea scroll addition about Shishak, see the variant.
r: Song of Songs 4:4; Jeremiah 51:11; Ezekiel 27:11; 2 Kings 11:10; 1 Chronicles 18:7

a: Toi, the king of Hamath
p: Hamath on the Orontes River was a powerful kingdom north of Zobah.
b: Hamath (modern Hama in Syria) was an enemy of Zobah. Its king welcomed David's victory and sent gifts, which implied friendship or submission. The son's name, Joram, contains the name of Israel's God; Chronicles calls him Hadoram, with the name of the storm god Hadad (1 Chronicles 18:10). He may have had two names, or taken a new one as a courtesy to David. "From Lebo-hamath" later marks Israel's northern border (1 Kings 8:65).

a: These King David set apart as holy for the LORD
p: David dedicated plunder to the LORD. Chronicles says it later went into Solomon's temple.
b: To dedicate (hiqdish) was to make holy, to give to God. David stores silver, gold and bronze for the house his son will build (1 Chronicles 22:14; 1 Chronicles 26:26–27). Solomon brings these things into the temple treasury (1 Kings 7:51). Even David's wars serve the house of God.

a: David won fame as well
p: God promised David a great name (7:9). Here David makes one.
b: Literally "David made a name." The phrase picks up God's promise to make his name great (7:9). The victory itself is credited elsewhere to Abishai (1 Chronicles 18:12) and in a psalm title to Joab (Psalm 60:0, twelve thousand); ancient kings were credited with what their generals did. On "Edom" or "Aram," see the variant.

a: He kept practicing justice and righteousness
p: Mishpat and tsedaqah: the ideal of a king who protects the weak.
b: The pair mishpat and tsedaqah means fair judgment and right dealing, especially for the poor and helpless. It is what God wants from kings (Jeremiah 22:3, 22:15–16; Psalm 72:1–4) and what the coming son of David will bring (Isaiah 9:7; Jeremiah 23:5). The participle "was doing" suggests an ongoing practice. Coming right before chapter 11, this summary sets a standard David will soon break.
r: Jeremiah 22:3; Jeremiah 22:15–16; Jeremiah 23:5; Psalm 72:1–4; Isaiah 9:7; 1 Kings 10:9

a: kept the records
p: The mazkir was a high official: recorder, herald or royal spokesman.
b: Mazkir comes from zakhar, "remember." The office appears in every list of royal officials (20:24; 1 Kings 4:3; 2 Kings 18:18). Some compare the Egyptian royal herald who reported to the king and announced his orders. Tryggve Mettinger argued that David modeled his administration partly on Egypt's. A comparable list of officials comes in 20:23–26.

a: Zadok son of Ahitub
p: Zadok appears here without warning. His origin is debated.
b: Zadok will become the head of Israel's priesthood under Solomon (1 Kings 2:35), and his line served in the temple for centuries (Ezekiel 44:15). Here he is "son of Ahitub," which would make him a relative of Eli's house (1 Samuel 14:3; 1 Samuel 22:9). But God had promised to replace Eli's house with a faithful priest (1 Samuel 2:35), and Chronicles traces Zadok to Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chronicles 6:4–8). H. H. Rowley suggested that Zadok was the Jebusite priest of Jerusalem, kept on by David; others think he came from Hebron (1 Chronicles 12:28). The text gives no full answer.
r: 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Samuel 2:35; 1 Samuel 14:3; 1 Chronicles 6:4–8; 1 Chronicles 12:28; Ezekiel 44:15

a: The royal scribe was Seraiah
p: The scribe's name differs in every list: Seraiah, Sheva, Shisha, Shavsha.
b: The sofer was the king's secretary, in charge of letters and records. The name is Seraiah here, Sheva in 20:25, Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16, and Shisha (as father of Solomon's scribes) in 1 Kings 4:3. Some scholars suggest the name was foreign, perhaps Egyptian, and that Hebrew scribes spelled it in different ways. Others think different men are meant.

a: the Kerethites and Pelethites
p: Foreign mercenaries, probably Cretans and Philistines, who guarded the king.
b: The Kerethites were probably from Crete (Caphtor), the Philistines' homeland (Amos 9:7), and the Pelethites probably Philistines. They formed a guard loyal to the king rather than to any tribe, and they stood by David in Absalom's revolt and at Solomon's anointing (15:18; 20:7; 1 Kings 1:38). David had lived among them at Ziklag; 1 Samuel 30:14 speaks of "the Kerethite Negev." Benaiah, their commander, later replaces Joab as head of the army (1 Kings 2:35).

a: David's sons served as priests
p: The Hebrew says kohanim, "priests." Chronicles and the ancient translations softened it.
b: Only Levites of Aaron's line could be priests under the law (Numbers 3:10). So the statement surprised later readers. Chronicles says David's sons were "first in rank beside the king" (1 Chronicles 18:17). The Targum calls them "great men," and the Greek "court chiefs." Some scholars take the Hebrew at face value: in David's early kingdom the king and his sons held priestly roles, as David did in chapter 6, and as the Melchizedek tradition suggests (Psalm 110:4). Others think kohen here means a high official, as perhaps in 20:26 and 1 Kings 4:5.

a: show him loyal love because of Jonathan
p: Jonathan had asked David never to cut off his loyal love from his family.
b: Jonathan said to David, "Never cut your loyal love away from my family, even when the LORD has cut away David's enemies, every one, from the face of the ground" (1 Samuel 20:15), and David swore it (1 Samuel 20:17, 20:42). David had sworn the same to Saul (1 Samuel 24:21–22). Ancient kings commonly wiped out the families of the dynasty they replaced (1 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 10:11). David's question, "Is anyone left?" could sound like a threat; it turns into kindness.

a: a servant named Ziba
p: Ziba managed Saul's land. He will later accuse his master in Absalom's revolt.
b: Ziba was a na'ar, a servant or steward, of Saul's house, with fifteen sons and twenty servants of his own (9:10). He seems to have been running Saul's estate for himself. When David flees from Absalom, Ziba meets him with supplies and says Mephibosheth hoped to win back his grandfather's kingdom (16:1–4). Mephibosheth later says Ziba deceived David (19:24–30). Which of them told the truth is one of the book's open questions.

a: the loyal love of God
p: Hesed of God: loyalty such as God shows, or loyalty sworn before God.
b: "The hesed of God" can mean kindness that reflects God's own, or kindness promised by oath in God's name. Jonathan asked David for "the LORD's loyal love" (1 Samuel 20:14), and their covenant was made before the LORD (1 Samuel 20:42; 1 Samuel 23:18). David means to keep a sworn promise, and to treat Jonathan's son as God treats his own.

a: Lo-debar
p: A town in Gilead whose name can be read as "no thing." Amos makes a pun on it.
b: Lo-debar was east of the Jordan, near Mahanaim, where Saul's house had ruled (2:8). Its name may mean "no pasture"; read slightly differently, it sounds like "nothing" (lo davar). Amos mocks Israel for rejoicing over "Lo-debar," a nothing (Amos 6:13). Machir son of Ammiel, who sheltered Mephibosheth, will later bring supplies to David in flight (17:27–29), perhaps because of David's kindness here.

a: you will eat your meals at my table from now on
p: An honor and a pension. Some readers also see a way to keep Saul's heir under watch.
b: To eat at the king's table meant a place of honor and support from the palace (1 Kings 2:7; 1 Kings 4:27). Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, is given a seat at the Babylonian king's table for life, at the very end of Kings (2 Kings 25:29). Most readers see David's generosity and faithfulness to Jonathan. Some historians add that the last heir of Saul now lives where David can see him. Christian preachers have often seen Mephibosheth as a picture of grace: a lame man with nothing, called by the king and seated at his table because of another's covenant.

a: a dead dog like me
p: A phrase of deep self-humbling. David once used it of himself before Saul.
b: "Dog" was an insult (3:8), and a dead dog was the least of all. David called himself "a dead dog" when he pleaded with Saul (1 Samuel 24:14), and Abishai will call Shimei one (16:9). Mephibosheth's words show his fear: the grandson of the old king expects nothing from the new one. The verb "turn toward" means to look on with favor.

a: a little son called Mica
p: Through Mica, Saul's descendants lasted for generations.
b: Chronicles traces many generations from Micah, son of Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), into the time of the later kings (1 Chronicles 8:34–40; 1 Chronicles 9:40–44). So David's loyalty to Jonathan kept Saul's family alive, even after the Gibeonite executions (21:7–9). The list ends with "mighty men of valor, archers."

a: both of his feet were lame
t: A lame man in the king's house
p: The chapter ends on Mephibosheth's lameness, recalling the saying about the lame in 5:8.
b: Chapter 5 ended its account of Jerusalem with a saying: "No one blind or lame may come into the house" (5:8). Chapter 9 ends with a lame man eating at the king's table in Jerusalem every day. Many commentators have noticed the contrast. Whether the narrator meant it or not, David's loyalty to Jonathan overrides the saying of the conquest.

a: the Ammonite king died
p: The dead king was Nahash, Saul's enemy at Jabesh (1 Samuel 11).
b: Nahash besieged Jabesh-gilead and threatened to gouge out every man's right eye before Saul rescued the town (1 Samuel 11:1–11). As Saul's enemy, he may have helped David when Saul hunted him. Chronicles names him in this verse (1 Chronicles 19:1). His son Shobi will later bring supplies to David at Mahanaim (17:27). Ammon's capital was Rabbah, modern Amman in Jordan.

a: just as his father kept loyal love with me
t: What did Nahash do for David?
p: No earlier kindness is recorded. Readers guess at an alliance against Saul.
b: The text says Nahash showed hesed to David, but never says how. The usual guess is that the enemy of Saul became the friend of Saul's fugitive. A midrash says that when the king of Moab killed David's family, one brother escaped to Nahash, who sheltered him (Numbers Rabbah 14:1). The word hesed links this chapter to chapter 9: David shows loyal love to Saul's grandson and tries to show it to an Ammonite king. One offer is welcomed, the other insulted.

a: He shaved half the beard off each man
p: A beard was a man's honor. Cutting the robes exposed them like prisoners of war.
b: In Israel and its neighbors, a beard was a mark of manhood and dignity; to shave it was a sign of mourning or humiliation (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 48:37; Leviticus 19:27). Cutting the robes to the buttocks exposed the men as captives were led away naked (Isaiah 20:4). To insult a king's messengers was to insult the king. Hanun's act was close to a declaration of war.

a: Stay in Jericho
p: Jericho was the first town on the road back from Ammon.
b: Jericho lay just west of the Jordan on the route from Rabbah to Jerusalem. Joshua had cursed anyone who would rebuild it as a city (Joshua 6:26), and it was refounded under Ahab (1 Kings 16:34), but a small settlement could still exist there. David lets his envoys wait out of sight until their beards grew back, sparing them shame.

a: they had made themselves stink to David
p: A Hebrew idiom: to become hateful or offensive to someone.
b: The verb ba'ash means "to stink." Jacob complained that his sons had made him stink to the Canaanites (Genesis 34:30), and Israel "stank" to the Philistines after Saul's son attacked them (1 Samuel 13:4; compare 1 Samuel 27:12). The Ammonites knew they had provoked war. Chronicles adds that they paid a thousand talents of silver and hired thirty-two thousand chariots (1 Chronicles 19:6–7).

a: Aram of Beth-rehob and Aram of Zobah
p: Several small Aramean kingdoms in Syria joined Ammon against David.
b: The Arameans were peoples speaking Aramaic, settled in Syria in the 11th–10th centuries BC. Beth-rehob lay near Dan (Judges 18:28), Zobah in the Beqaa Valley (8:3), Maacah near Mount Hermon (Joshua 13:13), and Tob east of the Jordan, where Jephthah once fled (Judges 11:3). Hadadezer of Zobah led them (10:16). David had already beaten him (8:3–8); chapters 8 and 10 may describe the same wars from two angles.

a: The LORD will do whatever he sees is good
p: Joab, ruthless elsewhere, speaks words of trust before battle.
b: Joab urges courage "for our people and our God's cities" and leaves the outcome to the LORD. Eli said something like it when Samuel told him God's judgment (1 Samuel 3:18). Readers have admired the balance: do your utmost, and trust God with the result. It is striking in the mouth of Joab, whose violence the book does not hide (3:27; 18:14; 20:10).

a: from the far side of the River
p: "The River" in the Bible usually means the Euphrates.
b: Hadadezer called up Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, showing how far his power reached (8:3). Helam was probably in northern Transjordan; a place called Alema east of the Sea of Galilee has been suggested. The commander's name is Shobach here and Shophach in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 19:16).

a: seven hundred of Aram's chariot drivers and forty thousand of its horsemen
t: The numbers in Samuel and Chronicles
p: Chronicles has seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers.
b: 1 Chronicles 19:18 reads "seven thousand" charioteers and forty thousand "foot soldiers." Numbers in Samuel and Chronicles often differ (compare 8:4 with 1 Chronicles 18:4), and numbers were easily miscopied. Some scholars think elef, usually "thousand," could also mean a military unit, which would make the figures much smaller. The Plain follows the Hebrew of Samuel here.

a: After that Aram was afraid
p: With Aram beaten, Ammon is left alone. The war with Ammon goes on in chapter 11.
b: The Arameans become David's vassals (8:6), and Ammon loses its allies. In spring Joab will besiege Rabbah, while David stays in Jerusalem (11:1). The war that began with David's kindness to Hanun becomes the setting for his sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah. The siege ends in 12:26–31.
